attackPath.dataflow: Untrusted content read by the model (repository file, web page, subagent output) -> prompt injection -> model emits a Bash tool call -> PreToolUse payload .tool_input.command -> validate-bash.sh regex classification -> permissionDecision.
attackPath.reachability: The hook runs on every Bash tool call, so the vulnerable classifier is always on the path. Reaching destructive execution additionally requires the base permission layer not to prompt.

codeEvidence.code:
if echo "$CMD" | grep -qE '(rm[[:space:]]+-rf[[:space:]]+/[^a-zA-Z]|rm[[:space:]]+-rf[[:space:]]+\$HOME|rm[[:space:]]+-rf[[:space:]]+~(/|$|[[:space:]])|sudo[[:space:]]+rm|:\(\)\{[[:space:]]*:\|:&[[:space:]]*\};:)'; then
  deny "Dangerous command pattern blocked: potential system damage ..."
fi
codeEvidence.explanation: The slash branch hardcodes the `-rf` bundle and ends in `[^a-zA-Z]`, which must consume a character. The sibling tilde branch in the same alternation uses `~(/|$|[[:space:]])` and does accept end-of-input. That inconsistency is the defect: the slash branch cannot match a command that ends immediately after the slash, and neither branch models any spelling other than `-rf`.
codeEvidence.label: Catastrophic-command deny regex

codeEvidence.explanation: The fallback that would otherwise downgrade an unmatched destructive command to `ask` enumerates only the short bundles `-r`, `-rf` and `-fr`. A long-form `--recursive --force` invocation matches neither this extractor nor the deny regex, so the hook emits no decision at all for it.
codeEvidence.label: Secondary ask-level target extractor

confidence.rationale: Bypass reproduced by feeding crafted payloads directly to the hook and reading the emitted permissionDecision; the deny/ask/none split is observed, not inferred.

preventiveControls: Classify shell commands on a parsed argv representation, never on raw text.
Every denylist clause needs a table-driven test enumerating equivalent spellings of the same dangerous operation.
findings.remediation: Normalise the command to argv before classifying instead of pattern-matching raw text: reuse the existing lib/is-true-flag.sh shlex-aware helper to detect recursive+force semantics regardless of spelling (-r, -R, --recursive, -f, --force, bundled or split), then test the resolved target. As a minimum immediate fix, anchor the slash branch as `/([^a-zA-Z]|$)` and cover the -fr, -r -f and long-form spellings.
remediationTests: Add a table-driven case to hooks/tests/validate-bash.test.sh asserting permissionDecision == deny for each spelling: `rm -rf /`, `rm -rf /*`, `rm -fr /*`, `rm -r -f /*`, `rm --recursive --force /*`, `rm --recursive --force ~`.
Add a negative control asserting that a command merely mentioning the pattern in a quoted commit message body is NOT denied, so the fix does not regress the existing message-body handling.
findings.rootCause: The alternation `rm[[:space:]]+-rf[[:space:]]+/[^a-zA-Z]` encodes one specific flag spelling and requires a character to follow the slash. `[^a-zA-Z]` consumes a character rather than permitting end-of-input, so the bare form cannot match. The adjacent `~` branch in the very same regex is written `~(/|$|[[:space:]])` and does anchor on `$` — that internal inconsistency shows the missing `$` in the `/` branch is an oversight, not a deliberate choice. The secondary ask-level clause at line 195 extracts targets with `rm[[:space:]]+-(r|rf|fr)[[:space:]]+`, which likewise cannot see long-form flags, so both layers miss the same spellings.

severity.changeConditions: Rises to high or critical if the ambient permission posture stops prompting for Bash(rm:*) — an unattended or auto-approving session, a broadened allow-list, or any future hook that auto-allows long-form flags. This repository explicitly runs 24/7 autonomous sessions, so that posture is a live configuration, not a hypothetical.
severity.rationale: Reproduced directly against the hook: `rm -rf /*` returns deny, while `rm --recursive --force /*` returns no decision at all and the bare `rm -rf /` form returns only ask. Impact if reached is destruction of the user's filesystem. It is not critical because this hook is defence-in-depth by its own header comment, and rm-safe-allowlist.sh correctly defers rather than auto-allowing these forms, so the command still falls through to the base Bash(rm:*) ask rule — an attended operator would still be prompted.

findings.summary: The hard-deny regex that is supposed to stop catastrophic filesystem destruction matches only the literal short-flag bundle `-rf` followed by a character. Equivalent invocations with identical destructive effect — `--recursive --force`, `-fr`, `-r -f`, and the bare `rm -rf /` form at end of input — are not matched, so the guard emits `ask`, or no decision at all, instead of `deny`.
findings.title: Catastrophic-command denylist is bypassed by equivalent flag spellings, downgrading deny to ask or to no decision

validation.method: Direct execution of the hook with crafted PreToolUse payloads, reading the emitted permissionDecision.

attackPath.dataflow: Local process as another uid pre-creates /tmp/claude-notify.log as a symlink -> notification hook fires -> the append follows the symlink -> write into the attacker-chosen file as the invoking user.
attackPath.reachability: Requires local code execution under a different uid on the same host; no remote path.

confidence.rationale: Paths and the append are read directly from source; /tmp permissions verified on the live host.

preventiveControls: Never use a fixed name directly under /tmp for a file the process will write; prefer $TMPDIR or an application-owned directory.
findings.remediation: Place both files under a user-owned directory such as $TMPDIR (per-user on macOS) or ~/.claude/logs, create the directory with mode 700, and do not follow symlinks when opening.
remediationTests: Pre-create the target path as a symlink to a canary file, run the hook, and assert the canary is unchanged.
findings.rootCause: LOG_FILE and DEBOUNCE_FILE are fixed literals under the shared /tmp root rather than a per-user directory or an O_NOFOLLOW/mktemp-created file, so the hook cannot distinguish its own file from an attacker-planted symlink of the same name.

severity.changeConditions: Rises if the host is shared or multi-user, if the log path is later consumed by anything that parses or executes it, or if a future writer truncates rather than appends.
severity.rationale: Confirmed world-writable sticky /tmp (drwxrwxrwt) and a real append at line 88. Impact is limited to appending attacker-influenceable log text or updating an mtime, not arbitrary content control, and it requires a hostile local process under a different uid — uncommon on a single-user developer workstation.

findings.summary: The notification hook writes its log and debounce lock to hardcoded `/tmp` paths. `/tmp` is world-writable on macOS, so a process running as another uid can pre-create either path as a symlink and have the hook's append or touch follow it, writing to a file of the attacker's choosing with the invoking user's privileges.
findings.title: Notification hook appends to fixed, predictable paths in world-writable /tmp

validation.method: Source review plus live verification of /tmp permissions.
